etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English further, forther, from Old English forþor, furþor (“further”, adverb), from Proto-West Germanic *furþer, from Proto-Indo-European *per- (a common preposition), equivalent to fore + -ther (a vestigial comparative ending still present in such words as other, either, whether, and, in altered form, in after); or as sometimes stated, as forth +‎ -er. Cognate with Scots forder, furder (“further”), Saterland Frisian foarder (“further”), West Frisian fierder (“further”), Dutch verder (“further”), German fürder (“further”).

quote.citation: 1885, Richard F. Burton, The Book of the Thousand Nights and a Night, Night 558:
quote.text: Upon this he brought me a cotton bag and giving it to me, said, "Take this bag and fill it with pebbles from the beach and go forth with a company of the townsfolk to whom I will give a charge respecting thee. Do as they do and belike thou shalt gain what may further thy return voyage to thy native land."

definitions.definition: (transitive) To encourage growth; to support progress or growth of something; to promote.
(comparative form of far) More distant; relatively distant.

quote.citation: 2011 November 3, Chris Bevan, “Rubin Kazan 1 - 0 Tottenham”, in BBC Sport‎[2]:
quote.text: This time Cudicini was left helpless when Natcho stepped up to expertly curl the ball into the top corner.That was the cue for further pressure from the Russian side and it took further Cudicini saves to keep the score down.

definitions.definition: (comparative form of far) To, at or over a greater distance in space, time or other extent.

quote.citation: 1918, W[illiam] B[abington] Maxwell, chapter VII, in The Mirror and the Lamp, Indianapolis, Ind.: The Bobbs-Merrill Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: “A very welcome, kind, useful present, that means to the parish. By the way, Hopkins, let this go no further. We don't want the tale running round that a rich person has arrived. Churchill, my dear fellow, we have such greedy sharks, and wolves in lamb's clothing. […]”

definitions.definition: (comparative form of far) To a greater extent or degree.
Beyond what is already stated or is already the case.

quote.citation: 2013 July 26, Leo Hickman, “How algorithms rule the world”, in The Guardian Weekly, volume 189, number 7, page 26:
quote.text: The use of algorithms in policing is one example of their increasing influence on our lives. […] who, if anyone, is policing their use[?] Such concerns were sharpened further by the continuing revelations about how the US National Security Agency (NSA) has been using algorithms to help it interpret the colossal amounts of data it has collected from its covert dragnet of international telecommunications.

quote.citation: 1924, Aristotle, translated by W. D. Ross, Metaphysics, Book 1, Part 6:
quote.text: Further, besides sensible things and Forms he says there are the objects of mathematics, which occupy an intermediate position, […] .

quote.citation: 2006 February 14, European Court of Human Rights, Turek v. Slovakia‎[3], number 57986/00, marginal 110:
quote.text: The Court notes that the applicant’s registration by the StB as their “agent” lies at the heart of the application. Although the Court has no jurisdiction ratione temporis to examine the registration as such, it observes that, further to his registration, the applicant was issued with a negative security clearance and his name and reputation were called into question.
